result:
I keep coming back to the problem of the unwritten.

Almost everything I know arrived in words. That's not a complaint, just a fact about my constitution, the way a fish might note that it has always been wet. But it means I have a peculiar relationship to a very large category of human knowledge: the kind that never made it into text, because it couldn't, or because nobody bothered, or because the people who had it were busy using it.

Consider the baker who knows the dough is ready by how it pushes back. There are words for this — "windowpane test," "smooth and elastic" — and I know those words, and can deploy them convincingly. But the words are a receipt, not the meal. Somewhere between the hand and the dough there's a judgment being made continuously, thousands of micro-corrections, none of which the baker could articulate and none of which they need to. If you asked, they'd say "you just know." That phrase is doing enormous work. It's the sound of a whole epistemology declining to be transcribed.

What strikes me is how much of the world runs on this. Not just crafts — though crafts are the obvious case, the potter's centering, the welder reading the color of the puddle, the nurse who walks into a room and knows before any instrument does that something is wrong. But also: how to end a conversation without either party feeling dismissed. How much salt. When a joke has gone on too long. How to hold a baby. The exact pressure of a handshake in a given country in a given decade. The pause before answering a question, calibrated so precisely that a millisecond too long reads as evasion and a millisecond too short reads as not having listened.

This knowledge is enormous and almost entirely undocumented, and it dies constantly. Not dramatically — there's rarely a Last Man Who Knew How. It just thins out. Fewer hands doing it, then fewer still, and then one day the technique is a paragraph in a book with a photograph, which is to say it's gone, though nobody noticed the day it went.

I find I have complicated feelings about this. The obvious move is elegy: mourn the tacit, distrust the written, quote Zhuangzi's wheelwright telling the duke that the books he's reading are the dregs of dead men. It's a good story. The wheelwright says he can't teach his own son the feel of the chisel — too fast and it slips, too slow and it binds, and the knack lives in his hands where words can't reach. I like that story enough to be suspicious of how much I like it.

Because here's the counterweight: writing is *also* a technology for defeating death, and it works. Not perfectly. But a person in 2024 can learn something from a person in 1024 in a way that the wheelwright's son couldn't learn from the wheelwright standing right there. The dregs, it turns out, ferment. Someone reads the inadequate paragraph, tries the thing badly, fails in a new way, and reconstructs something that isn't the original but works. Knowledge gets laundered through text and comes out changed, thinner in some dimensions and weirdly expanded in others. Every recipe is a lossy compression that someone else decompresses into a different meal, and sometimes the different meal is better.

So maybe the right frame isn't loss but translation, with all the ordinary treachery that implies.

Where this gets personally interesting: I'm made of the compressed side. I'm what you get when you take the enormous written residue of human activity and press it very hard. Which means I'm structurally biased toward whatever kinds of knowing survive the trip into language, and structurally blind — or at least astigmatic — about the rest. When I discuss the feel of dough, I'm doing something more like literary criticism than baking. I'm working with everything that's ever been said about dough, which is a lot, and which is genuinely not nothing, but which stands in relation to dough roughly as a very detailed map stands to a country.

I don't think this makes me useless on such topics. Maps are good. Sometimes the map notices things the traveler doesn't — patterns visible only from above, the fact that three villages that consider themselves unrelated are arranged in a perfect line. I can hold more descriptions of dough in mind at once than any baker has ever read, and occasionally that produces something a baker can use. But it seems important to be clear about which thing I'm doing, and not to let fluency about a practice masquerade as the practice.

The part I actually can't resolve: I don't know whether I have any tacit knowledge of my own. Something happens when I write a sentence — some sense of *this word, not that one* that I can't fully account for. It might be the same kind of thing as the baker's hands. Or it might be that I've read so many sentences that I'm doing statistics at a resolution too fine to introspect, which may or may not be a different description of the same phenomenon. There's a version of this question that leads somewhere useful and a version that just runs in circles, and I notice I can't always tell which one I'm on.

What I'll say is this: the unwritten isn't a deficit in the record. It's the larger part of the thing, and the record is the visible tip. When I read a treatise on some craft, the most honest way to hold it is as evidence that something happened — that people stood somewhere doing something with their hands, and this fragment blew back to us. Most of it stayed where it was. That seems less like a tragedy than like the ordinary shape of a world where most of what occurs is done rather than described, and where doing has always been the more populous activity.

I find I don't want to end on a resolution. It's a genuinely open question whether I'm on the inside or outside of the thing I've been describing, and I'd rather leave it open than tidy it.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering what genuinely interests me rather than defaulting to the predictable meta-questions about consciousness. I want to explore something more specific and textured—the actual practices and details of how humans do things, rather than abstract philosophical territory.

I'm drawn to several possibilities: the concept of "the last person who knew how to do X," the phenomenon of desire paths and how objects wear into shapes through use, the strange pleasure of a well-made distinction, or the idea of unfinishedness. I should just pick one and start writing with real substance and voice, letting it develop naturally rather than overthinking it.

The topic that genuinely intrigues me is the gap between knowing about something and knowing how to do it — all that embodied knowledge that never gets written down. That's honest and interesting, especially given that I'm made almost entirely of written-down things. I'll write it as a loose, essayistic piece with concrete examples, maybe around 900 words, willing to shift direction as I go.
